title: Step-wise Rubric Rewards for LLM Reasoning
claim: Rollout steps are scored against instance-specific rubrics from an LLM judge, then normalized and combined with outcome rewards for finer credit assignment.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, rubric generation feeding the training loop above
description: Two stacked rounded panels. The top panel shows the SRaR training loop. A Policy πθ and a Question x feed rollouts O1..On. Each rollout is a row of colored step chips (green correct, red flawed, yellow bonus) ending in a check or cross for the outcome. A legend (SUGGEST, PITFALL, BONUS) and an 'LLM as judge' arrow link the grading rubric to the steps. On the right, blue Outcome Reward and green Process Reward boxes hold normalization equations. Both feed a row of gray and purple token squares and a combined advantage formula. The bottom panel, 'Rubrics Generation Pipeline', starts with a math question and a proprietary model that produces correct and flawed outputs. A big arrow labeled Rubrics Distillation leads to a color-coded grading rubric with suggest, pitfall, bonus and answer sections. A connector returns to the top panel.
caption: Overview of SRaR. Top: The SRaR training framework. An LLM judge attributes each rubric item to a specific reasoning step; per-step rewards are normalized across rollouts and combined with outcome rewards via a decoupled advantage estimator. Bottom: The three-stage contrastive rubric distillation pipeline that generates instance-specific rubrics from correct and flawed paths.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning using final-answer correctness, but lacks supervision for intermediate steps. Rubric-based methods such as Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) provide finer-grained criteria, yet collapse rubric scores into a response-level scalar. This loses criterion-level structure, rewards flawed steps in correct responses, penalizes valid steps in incorrect responses, and can encourage unbounded self-correction. In 1,000 sampled problems, 18.2% of steps in answer-correct responses are wrong, while 49.9% of steps in answer-incorrect responses are correct. We propose Step-wise Rubrics as Rewards (SRaR), which (i) uses an LLM judge to assign rubric items to reasoning steps, (ii) normalizes step scores across rollouts to focus learning on quality differences, and (iii) combines step-wise and outcome rewards through a decoupled advantage estimator that preserves a stable outcome baseline. We also construct a 16K-problem rubric dataset by contrastively distilling criteria from verified correct and flawed reasoning paths. Across six math benchmarks, SRaR improves average accuracy over RaR by 3.57 and 2.75 points on Qwen3-8B-Non-Thinking and Qwen3-32B-Non-Thinking, respectively. On AIME 2025, it increases the Faithful Reasoning Rate from 34.5% to 46.7% and reduces self-correction looping from 48.1% to 26.5%. SRaR also achieves the best results on three of four code-generation benchmarks.
